source_refs.note: Book p. 61-64: 2.13 Error in Differential Approximations, error / relative error / percentage error, Examples 25-29

blocks.text: Suppose \(f\) is a differentiable function at a point \(x\), and there is a small change \(\Delta x\) in \(x\). If:

items: \(\Delta y\) is actual corresponding change in \(y\), given by \(\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\)
\(dy\) is the approximation change in \(y\) obtained using differentials, given by \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\) where \(dx = \Delta x\)

blocks.text_alt: Error equals delta y minus d y

blocks.latex: \text{Relative Error} = \dfrac{\Delta y - dy}{\Delta y} = \dfrac{\text{Error}}{\text{Original Value}},\ \Delta y \ne 0
blocks.text_alt: Relative error equals (delta y minus d y) over delta y, which is error over original value, when delta y is not zero
Percentage error equals the absolute value of (delta y minus d y) over delta y, times 100, when delta y is not zero

blocks.text: that is, Percentage Error \(= \left|\frac{\text{Error}}{\text{Original value}}\right| \times 100\) when \(\Delta y \ne 0\).

Error measures how far the easy estimate \(dy\) is from the true change \(\Delta y\).
Relative error compares the error with the size of the true change: an error of 0.03 is small if \(\Delta y = 100\) but large if \(\Delta y = 0.3\).
Percentage error is the relative error written per hundred, always positive (absolute value).
blocks.title: Teaching note
Example 25
blocks.problem: Find \(dy\) and \(\Delta y\) for the function \(f(x) = x^{3}\) when \(x = 1\) and \(dx = 0.1\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^{3}\), \(x = 1\), \(dx = \Delta x = 0.1\).
To find: the differential \(dy\) and the actual change \(\Delta y\).
Method: \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\) (tangent-line change) and \(\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\) (actual change).

Step 1: Differentiate
\[f(x) = x^{3} \quad \text{...(1)}\]
\[f'(x) = 3x^{2}\]
Why: power rule.

Step 2: Find \(dy\)
\[dy = f'(x)\,dx = 3x^{2}\,dx\]
\[dy = 3(1)^{2}(0.1) = 0.3\]
Why: substitute \(x = 1\) and \(dx = 0.1\) in the formula for \(dy\).

Step 3: Find \(\Delta y\)
\[\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\]
\[= f(1 + 0.1) - f(1)\]
\[= f(1.1) - f(1)\]
\[= (1.1)^{3} - (1)^{3}\]
\[= 1.331 - 1 = 0.331\]
Why: from equation (1), \(f(x) = x^{3}\); the actual change is new value minus old value, with \(\Delta x = dx = 0.1\).

Check (the error, using the definitions above):
\[\text{Error} = \Delta y - dy = 0.331 - 0.3 = 0.031\]
\[\left|\dfrac{0.031}{0.331}\right| \times 100 \approx 9.37\%\]
\(dy\) is close to \(\Delta y\); the error is the part the tangent line misses because the curve bends.

blocks.title: Example 26
steps:
Given: the number \(\sqrt{24}\).
To find: an approximate value without a calculator.
Method: \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy\) with \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\). Start from the nearest perfect square, 25, where \(\sqrt{25} = 5\) is exact.

Step 1: Choose the function and differentiate
\[f(x) = \sqrt{x} \quad \text{...(1)}\]
\[f'(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}x^{-1/2} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}\) and the power rule.

Step 2: Choose \(x\) and \(\Delta x\)
Choose a real number that closest to 24 is a perfect square. Take \(x = 25\).
We are approximating \(\sqrt{24}\), so: \(x + \Delta x = 24\) and \(x = 25\).
Thus: \(24 + \Delta x = 25 \Rightarrow \Delta x = -1\)
Since in differential approximation, \(dx = \Delta x\), we take: \(dx = -1\).
Why: 25 is the perfect square nearest to 24. \(\Delta x\) is negative because we move down from 25 to 24.

Step 3: Find \(dy\)
\[dy = f'(x)\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,dx\]
\[dy = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{25}}(-1)\]
\[= -\dfrac{1}{10} = -0.1\]
Why: from equation (2), with \(x = 25\) and \(dx = -1\).

Step 4: Use \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy\)
\[f(25 - 1) \approx f(25) + (-0.1)\]
\[f(24) \approx f(25) - 0.1\]
From equation (1):
\[\sqrt{24} = \sqrt{25} - 0.1 = 5 - 0.1 = 4.9\]
Why: the known value \(f(25) = 5\) plus the small correction \(dy\).

Check:
\[4.9^{2} = 24.01\]
Very close to 24. Calculator: \(\sqrt{24} = 4.89898\), so the error is only about \(0.001\).

blocks.text:
Example 26 prints \(24 + \Delta x = 25 \Rightarrow \Delta x = -1\). From \(x + \Delta x = 24\) with \(x = 25\) the equation is \(25 + \Delta x = 24\), which gives \(\Delta x = -1\) (the printed equation would give \(+1\)).
The final line prints \(\sqrt{24} = \sqrt{25} - 0.1\); since this is an approximation it should be \(\sqrt{24} \approx 4.9\).
blocks.title: Book correction
Example 27
blocks.problem: Using differentials approximate the value of \(\cos 61^\circ 3\).
steps:
Given: \(\cos 61^\circ\) (the printed "3" is a stray character; see the correction below).
To find: an approximate value of \(\cos 61^\circ\).
Method: \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy\) with \(f(x) = \cos x\), starting at \(60^\circ\), whose cosine and sine are known exactly. \(dx\) must be in radians.

Step 1: Choose the function and differentiate
\[f(x) = \cos x \quad \text{...(1)}\]
\[f'(x) = -\sin x \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: standard derivative of cosine.

Step 2: Choose \(x\) and \(\Delta x\)
Choose \(x = 60^\circ\) because calculating \(\cos 60^\circ\) is easy.
\[x + \Delta x = 61^\circ,\ x = 60^\circ\]
\[60^\circ + \Delta x = 61^\circ \Rightarrow \Delta x = 1^\circ\]
\[dx = 1^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{180} \text{ radian}\]
Why: in differential approximation \(dx = \Delta x\), and the derivative formula of \(\cos x\) holds only for radians.

Step 3: Find \(dy\)
\[dy = f'(x)\,dx = -\sin x\,dx\]
\[dy = -\sin 60^\circ\left(\dfrac{\pi}{180}\right)\]
\[= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{\pi}{180}\]
\[= -0.0151\]
Why: from (2) with \(x = 60^\circ\) and \(dx = \frac{\pi}{180}\); \(\sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.017453\).

Step 4: Use \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy\)
\[f(61^\circ) \approx f(60^\circ) + (-0.0151)\]
From equation (1):
\[\cos 61^\circ = \cos 60^\circ - 0.0151\]
\[= 0.5 - 0.0151 = 0.4849\]
Why: \(\cos 60^\circ = 0.5\) exactly (the result is approximate, \(\cos 61^\circ \approx 0.4849\)); \(dy\) is negative because cosine decreases between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\).

Check:
Calculator: \(\cos 61^\circ = 0.48481\). The estimate \(0.4849\) differs by less than \(0.0001\).

blocks.text: Example 27 prints "approximate the value of \(\cos 61^\circ 3\)". The "3" is a stray character: the solution approximates \(\cos 61^\circ\) (\(\approx 0.4849\)). The final line also prints "\(\cos 61^\circ = \ldots\)" for a value that is only approximate (\(\approx\)).
blocks.title: Book correction

blocks.text:
Examples 28 and 29 use "error" in a second, practical sense: an error in measuring a quantity (here the side or radius, \(dx\) or \(dr\)) causes an error in a quantity calculated from it (volume, area), estimated by its differential (\(dV\), \(dA\)).
Percentage error in a calculated quantity \(Q\): \(\left|\frac{dQ}{Q}\right| \times 100\).
Shortcut: if \(Q = kx^{n}\), then \(\frac{dQ}{Q} = n\frac{dx}{x}\): the percentage error is multiplied by the power \(n\) (cube volume: 3 times; circle area: 2 times; circumference: 1 time).
blocks.title: Teaching note
Example 28
blocks.problem:
The side of a cube is measured to be 25 cm, with a possible error of \(\pm 1\) cm.
(a) Use differentials to estimate the error in the calculated volume.
(b) Estimate the percentage errors in the side and volume.
steps:
Given: side \(x = 25\) cm, error in the side \(dx = \Delta x = \pm 1\) cm.
To find: (a) the error \(dV\) in the volume; (b) the percentage errors in the side and in the volume.
Method: the error in a calculated quantity is estimated by its differential: \(V = x^{3}\), so \(dV = 3x^{2}\,dx\).

(a) Step 1: The differential of \(V\)
\[V = x^{3}\]
\[dV = \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{3})\,dx\]
\[= 3x^{2}\,dx \quad \text{...(1)}\]
Why: a small error \(dx\) in the side causes a change of about \(dV\) in the volume.

Step 2: Substitute \(x = 25\), \(dx = \pm 1\) in (1)
\[dV = 3(25)^{2}(\pm 1)\]
\[= \pm 1875 \text{ cm}^{3}\]
Thus, the estimated error in measuring volume is \(\pm 1875\) cm\(^{3}\).
Why: \(25^{2} = 625\) and \(3 \times 625 = 1875\).

(b) Step 3: Percentage error in the side
\[\left|\dfrac{dx}{x}\right| \times 100 = \dfrac{1}{25} \times 100\]
\[= 4\% \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: percentage error = (error / measured value) \(\times\) 100.

Step 4: Percentage error in the volume
Since \(V = x^{3}\) and \(dV = 3x^{2}\,dx\):
\[\left|\dfrac{dV}{V}\right| \times 100 = \left|\dfrac{3x^{2}\,dx}{x^{3}}\right| \times 100\]
\[= 3 \times \left|\dfrac{dx}{x}\right| \times 100\]
Using equation (2):
\[\left|\dfrac{dV}{V}\right| \times 100 = 3 \times 4\% = 12\%\]
Why: \(\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3}} = \frac{1}{x}\), so the percentage error of the volume is 3 times that of the side.

Check:
\[V = 25^{3} = 15625 \text{ cm}^{3}\]
\[\dfrac{1875}{15625} \times 100 = 12\%\]
The same 12% comes directly from parts (a) and the volume.

blocks.title: Example 29
blocks.problem:
The radius \(r\) of a circle is measured with an error of at most 2%. What is the maximum corresponding percentage error in computing the circle's
(a) circumference? (b) area?
steps:
Given: percentage error in the radius \(\left|\frac{dr}{r}\right| \times 100 = 2\%\).
To find: the percentage error in (a) \(C = 2\pi r\) and (b) \(A = \pi r^{2}\).
Method: find the differential of each formula, divide by the formula itself, and use the given 2%. The radius itself is not needed.

Step 1: The given error
Since \(r\) is the radius, the percentage error in measuring the radius is
\[\left|\dfrac{dr}{r}\right| \times 100 = 2\% \quad \text{...(1)}\]

(a) Step 2: Differential of the circumference
\[C = 2\pi r\]
\[dC = \dfrac{d}{dr}(2\pi r)\,dr = 2\pi\,dr \quad \text{...(2)}\]
Why: \(2\pi\) is a constant, so the derivative of \(2\pi r\) is \(2\pi\).

Step 3: Percentage error in the circumference
\[\left|\dfrac{dC}{C}\right| \times 100 = \left|\dfrac{2\pi\,dr}{2\pi r}\right| \times 100\]
\[= \left|\dfrac{dr}{r}\right| \times 100\]
Using equation (1):
\[\left|\dfrac{dC}{C}\right| \times 100 = 2\%\]
Why: \(2\pi\) cancels; \(C\) is proportional to \(r\) (power 1), so its percentage error equals that of \(r\).

(b) Step 4: Differential of the area
\[A = \pi r^{2}\]
\[dA = \dfrac{d}{dr}(\pi r^{2})\,dr = 2\pi r\,dr\]
Why: power rule, \(\pi\) is a constant.

Step 5: Percentage error in the area
\[\left|\dfrac{dA}{A}\right| \times 100 = \left|\dfrac{2\pi r\,dr}{\pi r^{2}}\right| \times 100\]
\[= 2 \times \left|\dfrac{dr}{r}\right| \times 100\]
Using equation (1):
\[\left|\dfrac{dA}{A}\right| \times 100 = 2 \times 2\% = 4\%\]
Why: \(\frac{r}{r^{2}} = \frac{1}{r}\); power 2 doubles the percentage error.

Check with numbers (any radius works), say \(r = 10\), \(dr = 0.2\) (2%):
\[dA = 2\pi(10)(0.2) = 4\pi,\ A = 100\pi\]
\[\dfrac{4\pi}{100\pi} \times 100 = 4\%\]

blocks.text:
1. Error \(= \Delta y - dy\); relative error \(= \frac{\Delta y - dy}{\Delta y}\); percentage error \(= \left|\frac{\Delta y - dy}{\Delta y}\right| \times 100\).
2. To approximate a value: \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,dx\), starting from a nearby easy value.
3. For angles, \(dx\) must be in radians: \(1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}\).
4. Measurement error: \(dQ = Q'(x)\,dx\); percentage error \(\left|\frac{dQ}{Q}\right| \times 100\).
5. For \(Q = kx^{n}\), percentage error in \(Q\) = \(n \times\) percentage error in \(x\).
blocks.title: Key points

blocks.text:
1. Putting \(dx = 1\) for \(1^\circ\); it must be \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
2. Wrong sign of \(\Delta x\): moving from 25 down to 24 gives \(\Delta x = -1\).
3. Writing \(=\) for an approximate value.
4. Forgetting the absolute value, giving a negative percentage error.
5. Adding the percentage errors instead of multiplying by the power.
blocks.title: Common mistake
